intro: Before the First World War, the managers of the Auersberg estate tried to kill this oak by stripping away dozens of cartloads of soil from around its roots. It survived, and in 2024 the country voted it Czech Tree of the Year. It grows on the open ground of a former fortress at Lukavice, more than seven metres round and estimated at nearly 800 years old. About 24 kilometres away at Zamrsk stands the other winner: a lime that came back as six trunks from one cut stump, voted Tree of the Year nine years earlier.
meta_description: The Lukavický dub, Czech Tree of the Year 2024, is a 700cm oak on a former fortress site, nearly 800 years old, once targeted for a slow death.
question_meta: Lukavice's ancient tree is a 700cm oak, nearly 800 years old, voted Czech Tree of the Year in 2024. It once survived a deliberate attempt to kill it.
question_answer: The Lukavický dub is an oak on the open ground of a former fortress at Lukavice, its trunk exceeding seven metres round and estimated at nearly 800 years old. In 2024 it was voted Czech Tree of the Year.
question_context: The oak grows where a fortress belonging to the local Auersberg estate once stood, in what was its courtyard. Before the First World War the estate's own management reportedly tried to kill the tree by stripping dozens of cartloads of soil away from its roots; it survived regardless, and stands today at more than seven metres round and 31 metres tall. Eight centuries of standing still has turned it into more than a tree: it now carries its own fungi, beetles and bats, most needing wood that has been dead a long time inside a trunk that is still alive. It has been legally protected since 1990, and in 2024 the country voted it Czech Tree of the Year. The sources call it simply dub, oak, without naming the species further; if you can tell a pedunculate from a sessile by the acorn stalks, tell us which this is. It stands on open community ground in the village of Lukavice, free at any time.

faq.q: How old is the Lukavický dub?
faq.a: Estimated at nearly 800 years, based on its size rather than a ring count; treat it as a wide estimate rather than a precise figure.

faq.q: What did the Auersberg estate do to it?
faq.a: Before the First World War, the estate's management reportedly stripped dozens of cartloads of soil from around its roots in a slow attempt to kill it. The tree survived.
January and February, when the bare branches show the whole frame of an 800-year-old tree.

trees.name: Lukavický dub (Dub na Hrádku / Dub u Lukavické tvrze)

location.address: On the open ground of a former fortress (Hrádek), Lukavice

trees.access: Free, on open community ground at the former fortress site
trees.story:
Somebody once tried to kill this oak with a shovel. Before the First World War the management of the Auersberg estate had dozens of cartloads of soil stripped away from around its roots, which is a slow and deniable way to finish a tree. It is still standing, and in 2024 the country voted it Czech Tree of the Year.

It grows on the open ground of the Hrádek at Lukavice, the site of a fortress belonging to the local nobility, and it stood in that courtyard while the courtyard was still a courtyard. The trunk is more than seven metres round and the tree is 31 metres tall. Its age is estimated at nearly 800 years, which would put its first seasons somewhere in the thirteenth century; that is an estimate rather than a count, and the honest band around it is wide.

Eight centuries of standing still has turned it into a habitat rather than a tree. It carries its own fungi, beetles and bats, most of which need wood that has been dead for a long time inside a tree that is still alive. It has been legally protected since 1990.

The sources call it dub, oak, and go no further. If you can tell a pedunculate from a sessile by the acorn stalks, tell us which this is.

best_time.label: January and February, when the leaves are off and the whole frame of it is readable

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by standing alone on the open ground of the former Hradek fortress, 7 metres round and 31 metres tall. It stands at Lukavice, where a stripped-bare root zone once nearly killed it.

trees.name: The Six-Trunked Lime of Zamrsk (Sestikmenna lipa v Zamrsku)

location.address: Castle park (zamecky park), Zamrsk, Usti nad Orlici District
location.neighbourhood: Zamrsk, about 4km northeast of Vysoke Myto

trees.access: Free, in the public castle park at Zamrsk, which also houses the regional state archive (Statni oblastni archiv) and serves as a recreation area for visitors. Reached via the blue-marked hiking trail from the Dobrikov u Chocne or Vysoke Myto train stations.
trees.transport: Nearest station Dobrikov u Chocne or Vysoke Myto, then the blue-marked hiking trail into the castle park.
trees.story:
Somebody cut this tree down, and it came back with six trunks. The original stem had gone hollow and was taken off; six shoots rose from the stump, and those are what stands in the castle park at Zamrsk today. One lime, six stems, about 25 metres tall. Czech Wikipedia puts each stem at over two metres round, turistika.cz measures them between two and four, and nobody has folded that into a single girth figure because there is no single trunk to measure.

Its age is not settled either. Wikipedia says more than 150 years, turistika.cz says roughly 200, and neither explains how it arrived at the number, so the honest answer is somewhere in that band. What is dated is 1995, when the growth form alone was enough to make it a pamatny strom, a protected tree.

Nine years later the pupils of the local primary school put it forward for Strom roku, the national Tree of the Year, and the country voted for it. That makes two winners within about 24 kilometres of each other, since the oak at Lukavice took the same title in 2024.

The park is public and doubles as the grounds of the regional state archive. Blue waymarks bring walkers in from the stations at Dobrikov u Chocne and Vysoke Myto. Standing under it, the six stems read as a small grove until you follow them down to one stump.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the six trunks rising from a single stump, each over two metres round and reaching about 25 metres. It stands in the castle park at Zamrsk, the park around the regional state archive.

best_time.label: June to July, when it flowers
